issues.legal_issue: An order disposing of an application for temporary injunctive relief is appealable when the trial court rejects the application on the ground that the injunction rule does not apply, even if the application also invokes inherent jurisdiction.
material_facts: The applicants sought a temporary injunction under the procedural rules for injunctions and also invoked the court’s inherent powers.
The trial court rejected the application on the ground that the complained-of harm did not fall within the injunction rule.
The appellate court declined to hear an appeal, reasoning that the trial court had acted under its inherent powers rather than under the injunction rules.
issues.conclusion: The order was appealable because the trial court had decided whether the application was competent under the injunction rule; the appellate court and the High Court erred in holding that no appeal lay.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 104 and Order XLIII Rule 1(r) of the Code of Civil Procedure, an appeal lies from an order under Order XXXIX Rules 1, 2, 4 or 10. When a court deciding an application for temporary injunction determines that the relief sought does not fall within Order XXXIX Rule 2, it is deciding the application under that rule, and the order is appealable. The inclusion of a request under Section 151 does not make the decision an exercise of inherent powers where the court has decided the scope of Order XXXIX Rule 2.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an order on a temporary injunction application and the trial court decided the scope of the injunction procedure, the order is appealable.

issues.legal_issue: A discretionary refusal of temporary injunctive relief should not be disturbed in special-leave review where the applicant has not shown a prima facie case, the balance of convenience favors the opposing party, and the trial court has not exercised its discretion arbitrarily or capriciously.
material_facts: The applicants’ application raising their claimed status under rent-control law had been dismissed, and they had not challenged that dismissal.
The opposing party denied that a landlord-and-tenant relationship existed with the applicants.
The trial court found that the applicants had been guilty of delay, that the balance of convenience favored the opposing party, and that the applicants had not established a prima facie case.
The Supreme Court found no capricious or arbitrary exercise of discretion by the trial court, although it held that the lower courts had erred in concluding that no appeal lay.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court did not interfere with the refusal of temporary injunctive relief and dismissed the appeal because the applicants had not established a prima facie case or shown grounds to disturb the trial court’s discretion.
issues.legal_principle: In exercising its power under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Court would not interfere with the trial court’s discretionary decision on temporary injunctive relief where no prima facie case was made out, the balance of convenience favored the opposing party, and the discretion was not exercised capriciously or arbitrarily. The Court also relied on the unchallenged dismissal of the applicants’ application under Section 4 of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, and the denial of a landlord-and-tenant relationship. The judgment cites no earlier case as authority for this conclusion.
